text: Look at any major city in Europe,
Australia, or South America right now.
You will see a new king taking over the
roads. Sleek, affordable, futuristic
electric vehicles bearing three letters,
BYD. The business world is calling them
the next Toyota. Harvard case studies
praise their vertical integration.
Wall Street marvels at its
record-breaking profit margins. But, if
you travel 5,000 mi away to the
outskirts of Hangzhou or Guangzhou, you
will find a very different reality. You
will find massive, overgrown fields
filled with thousands of brand-new,
unregistered BYD cars. They're left
there to quietly rot in the sun.
This is the greatest corporate illusion
of our time. How did a single company
convince the smartest investors on the
planet that they were a capitalist
miracle, while secretly running one of
the most sophisticated financial shell
games in modern history? We are going to
tear down the facade. We will look at
the phantom sales, the hidden debt, and
the staggering government machine
keeping it all afloat. The world is
being played. The story of BYD went
global around 2020, and it needed a
protagonist. It found one in Wang
Chuanfu,
a chemist turned billionaire from rural
Anhui province, who had started a
company in a rented warehouse, and grown
it into a global manufacturing giant.
The financial press loved him. Warren
Buffett had held BYD shares since 2008,
and in the world of investor signaling,
that single fact carried enormous
weight. If Buffett owns it, the thinking
went, it must be real. Harvard Business
School published case studies praising
the genius of BYD's vertical integration
model. Goldman Sachs analysts described
the stock as a generational opportunity.
The BBC ran feature profiles presenting
Wang Chuanfu as a reluctant visionary
who had simply outthought the
competition. Forbes listed him among the
world's wealthiest people, and framed
the wealth as earned through pure
engineering brilliance. None of those
institutions was lying on purpose. That
is what makes this so dangerous. They
were reading from a script that BYD had
spent 20 years writing for them. A
script with one central argument. This
was an organic miracle. A company that
had risen from a battery workshop to a
global automotive force through
discipline, scale, and ingenuity. A
David who had beaten Goliath by being
smarter.
By 2022, BYD overtook Tesla to become
the world's largest seller of new energy
vehicles. The financial world erupted in
applause. The underdog narrative was
complete. And at that exact moment,
while analysts were updating their price
targets, something else was happening
inside the company. Something that none
of those reports mentioned. The price of
winning was not what it appeared.
Consider one number. In early 2025, BYD
cut the starting price of its cheapest
model, the Seagull, to 55,800
yuan. That is roughly 5,800 British
pounds for a full electric vehicle,
complete with a screen, software, a
warranty, and a battery built from some
of the most expensive raw materials on
the planet. No Western automaker can
reach that number. Not Stellantis, not
Volkswagen, not Ford. The average cost
to manufacture a competitive electric
car in Europe or America sits somewhere
between 30,000 and 40,000 dollars before
you add logistics, dealer margin, or
profit. BYD is selling finished,
globally shipped cars at prices that
make those manufacturers look like
they're operating in a different
universe. The mainstream explanation is
vertical integration. BYD manufactures
its own batteries, cutting out the
middleman. And yes, that helps, but it
does not explain a gap this extreme.
When analysts model the battery cost
advantage honestly, the numbers still
don't add up. You're left staring at a
price point that pure engineering cannot
justify. Here is what makes the math
even harder to ignore. By 2024, only
three Chinese automakers were operating
in the black. The average profit per
electric vehicle across the entire
Chinese market had collapsed to around
2,000 yuan per unit. At those margins, a
sustained global pricing war should be
financially fatal for any company
running it. And yet, BYD keeps cutting
prices. So, the question is not how they
are winning. The question is who is
covering the bill? If this is landing
differently than you expected, hit
subscribe and turn on notifications.
What comes next makes the pricing story
look almost reasonable. Between 2018 and
2022, China's government transferred at
least 3.7 billion dollars directly into
BYD's accounts. According to research
published by Germany's Kiel Institute
for the World Economy, that support
jumped from around 220 million dollars
in 2020 to 2.1 billion dollars in 2022
alone. And that is only the direct
payment figure. It does not count
discounted or free land provided for
factory construction. It does not count
preferential access to raw materials. It
does not count the government
procurement policy that steered public
sector vehicle purchases toward BYD and
away from foreign competitors. It does
not count the purchase tax exemptions
worth up to 30,000 yuan per vehicle per
buyer, which made BYD products
artificially cheaper at the point of
sale. Most recently, in 2025, BYD
received 12.47 billion yuan in
government subsidies related to its
daily operations. That figure
represented 31.4% of its total pre-tax
profit. Strip those subsidies out
entirely, and BYD's adjusted net profit
would fall by roughly 50% from the prior
year. The company that the global press
celebrates as a capitalist miracle is,
in financial reality, a state project
wearing a corporate suit. Its pricing
strategy is not a competitive advantage.
It is a transfer of public money into
the private market destruction. And here
is the detail that rarely makes the
headline. The Kiel Institute found that
over 99% of listed Chinese companies
received direct government subsidies in
2022. This is not exceptional. It is the
infrastructure of the entire system.
What makes BYD different is not that it
receives state support. It is what that
support has been used to build. Not a
better product, a better illusion. And
the illusion only holds as long as
nobody looks at the balance sheet. In
January 2025, an accounting firm called
GMT Research published a report that
should have stopped the market cold. GMT
had previously issued warnings about
China Evergrande Group before its
catastrophic collapse. Now, they were
looking at BYD, and what they found was
a number that the company's own filings
had kept almost entirely out of sight.
BYD's official financial statements
listed net debt of 27.7 billion yuan as
of mid-2024.
GMT's analysis, working from the same
publicly available figures, put the
actual number closer to 323 billion
yuan. A discrepancy arising from the
company's practice of removing
receivables from its balance sheet, and
treating long-delayed supplier payments
as working capital rather than
liability. BYD runs a promissory note
platform called DiLink, through which it
pays suppliers not in cash, but in notes
redeemable at a later date. By May 2023,
the platform had issued approximately
400 billion yuan worth of these notes.
In 2023, BYD took an average of 275
days to pay its suppliers, compared to a
global industry norm of between 45 and
60 days. That gap is not operational
efficiency. That is a shadow banking
structure buried inside an automotive
company using the supply chain as a
lending mechanism. GMT described BYD
as appearing addicted to supply chain
financing. Chinese regulators responded
in early 2025 with new rules ordering
companies to settle supplier payments
within 60 days. The same firm that
identified the rot inside Evergrande is
now pointing at the same structural
pattern in a different sector with a
much bigger company. And the world's
financial press has barely noticed. Walk
into a used car dealership in China
today, and you might find something that
does not make sense. Rows of electric
vehicles with seat plastic still intact.
That specific smell only brand-new
interiors have. Zero kilometers on the
odometer, listed as used. Chinese
regulators summoned BYD and several
other major automakers to an inquiry
after investigations confirmed that
manufacturers were registering new
vehicles as sold to dealers on paper,
collecting government subsidies tied to
each unit, and then routing those cars
into the used market at heavily
discounted prices.
Subsidies designed to encourage clean
energy adoption could reach up to 30,000
yuan per vehicle.
Instead of reaching genuine buyers, the
scheme allowed manufacturers to pocket
the credit, then offload inventory they
had effectively sold to themselves.
Drone footage from sites near Hangzhou
and Wuhan showed vast open-air lots
filled with thousands of untouched
vehicles sitting idle in the open air.
Competitors saw it before regulators
did. The CEO of Great Wall Motor, Wei
Jianjun, gave an interview where he
explicitly referenced the Evergrande of
the auto industry without naming BYD
directly. Everyone who heard it
understood which company he was
describing. BYD's own dealer network
showed average inventory levels of 3.21
months per dealer, more than double the
industry benchmark of 1.38 months.
At least one large BYD dealer had
collapsed entirely with 20 or more of
its stores found closed or abandoned.
The sales figures said one thing. The
empty showrooms said everything else. On
December 19th, 2024, Brazilian labor
inspectors raided a construction site in
Camacari in the northeastern state of
Bahia. The site was being built for
BYD's first automobile factory in
Brazil. A project celebrated by the
Brazilian government as a symbol of
economic cooperation. Authorities
identified 471 Chinese workers who had
entered Brazil illegally. Of those, 163
were formally rescued from conditions
investigators classified as analogous to
slavery. Workers were sleeping in rooms
without mattresses. In one dormitory, 31
people shared a single bathroom, forcing
workers to queue at 4:00 a.m. to prepare
for shifts beginning at 5:30.
The workers' passports had been
confiscated, and 60% of their wages were
being withheld and sent back to China.
Those who tried to leave were told they
would owe the company for their flights
from China and would not receive a
return ticket home. A labor contract
reviewed by Reuters contained clauses
violating labor laws in both Brazil and
China, including provisions for
unilateral contract extensions and fines
for conduct as minor as swearing on
site.
BYD blamed a subcontractor. Brazilian
investigators concluded that BYD bore
direct responsibility for the illegal
entry of the workers into Brazil,
finding that in practice the workers
were directly subordinate to the
automaker despite the service contracts
presented.
In 2025, Brazil added BYD to its
official registry of employers who have
subjected workers to conditions
analogous to slavery. This is the human
cost of the cheapest cars on Earth, and
the people buying those cars in
showrooms around the world, they're
about to discover that the product
itself carries its own set of risks. By
November 2025, BYD had recalled more
than 210,000 vehicles in a single year.
In September 2024, the company recalled
Dolphin and Yuan Plus electric vehicles
due to a manufacturing fault in their
steering column control units that posed
a direct fire risk.
In January 2025, a further 6,843
Fangchengbao plug-in hybrid SUVs were
recalled, again citing fire hazards. In
October, BYD recalled a further 115,000
vehicles in what it described as its
largest recall to date. Weeks later came
an additional 89,000 Qin Plus hybrids
for battery pack inconsistencies severe
enough that some vehicles could not
operate in electric mode at all. The
pattern matters as much as the numbers.
Almost every recall involved the battery
or electrical system, the exact
technology BYD has spent 20 years
telling the world it has mastered. The
2025 Qin Plus recall was initiated by
Chinese regulators themselves, meaning
the defect was discovered by the
government rather than self-reported by
BYD. The company's competitive identity
rests entirely on the claim that its
blade battery technology is the safest
in the industry. Safety failures
originating in the battery system are
not peripheral problems. They are the
central promise of the company falling
apart from the inside. BYD reported its
second consecutive quarter of profit
decline in late 2025 with net income
falling 33% year over year. Revenue fell
for the first time in 5 years. The
miracle was beginning to show its seams,
and in Beijing the people who had built
that miracle were beginning to ask a
question they had spent years avoiding.
In 2021, the world watched China's
largest property developer, Evergrande,
collapse under 300 billion dollars of
hidden debt. The warning signs had been
visible for years. Inflated sales
figures, off-balance-sheet financing
structures, a business model requiring
perpetual growth held together by a
government that appeared unwilling to
let the structure fail until the moment
it was no longer able to hold it. Then
Beijing blinked. The support stopped,
and one of the largest corporate
collapses in history played out in
public. The structural parallels to what
is happening across China's electric
vehicle sector today are not subtle.
They are the same playbook running in a
different industry. In August 2025,
Chinese officials were reported to have
privately urged companies, including
BYD, to stop the price war before it
destroyed the entire sector. President
Xi Jinping himself criticized provincial
governments for blindly over-investing
in EV production capacity. Industry
consultancy AlexPartners predicted that
of China's roughly 130 electric vehicle
brands, only 15 would survive to 2030.
115 companies eliminated. BYD reported
its first annual profit decline since
2021 in its 2025 annual results. Strip
out government subsidies, and the real
profit is half of what is reported. The
wall of state capitalism can hold back
many things. It has not yet found a way
to hold back mathematics indefinitely.
Evergrande was also called too big to
fail. Its executives were also profiled
as visionaries. Its sales figures were
also cited as proof of an organic
miracle.
The CEO of Great Wall Motor was not
subtle about what he believed comes next
for an industry built on the same
foundations. And the people who will
feel it first are not in China at all.
This story is not about cars. It never
was. It is about a new method for using
state power as a competitive weapon, one
that has been refined across multiple
industries and is now sophisticated
enough to defeat the institutions the
West built to detect exactly this kind
of threat. Harvard case studies praised
it. Goldman Sachs analysts priced it as
a buy. Regulators missed it for years.
The same playbook used in electric
vehicles has already been deployed in
solar panels, semiconductors, steel, and
shipbuilding. The target is always the
same, the industries that underpin the
economic security of the country being
disrupted. The European Union imposed
tariffs of up to 38% on Chinese electric
vehicles in late 2024. The United States
raised its own tariffs to 100%. These
are not the actions of countries trying
to protect weak industries. They are the
actions of governments that were late to
understand the game being played and are
now scrambling to respond. The
individual cost is real, and it is
personal.
Pension funds hold BYD through green
energy ETFs and index funds. Retail
investors bought into the clean energy
narrative without auditing the
foundation it was built on. Every
portfolio carrying BYD exposure today is
sitting on a structure that the firm,
which has called Evergrande, has
publicly described as carrying hidden
debt 17 times larger than the company
reports.
The machine is visible now. The
subsidies, the phantom sales, the shadow
debt, the labor conditions, the recalls,
the Evergrande echo. You have seen the
architecture of the illusion from the
inside. The only question left is a
simple one. Now that you know how the
game works, are you still willing to
play by their rules?
